Steady Growth Continues in Finland’s Metals & Mining Trade Figures

Finland’s metals and mining sector reported stable trade figures for the second quarter of 2024, with export and import activity maintaining a consistent trajectory amid ongoing demand from European and Asian markets. According to preliminary data released Tuesday by the Finnish Chamber of Industry and Trade, overall exports of refined metals and raw minerals reached €1.42 billion between April and June, a modest 2.1% increase compared to the same period last year.

Industry analysts say the figures reflect the sector’s resilience and steady international demand, particularly for nickel, copper, and zinc concentrates. “We’re seeing a continuation of gradual growth, with no major disruptions or surprises,” said Sanni Hietala, senior analyst at the Helsinki-based consultancy Baltic Minerals Advisory. “This stability is positive for both producers and downstream industries.”

Imports of mining equipment and processing chemicals also registered a slight uptick, totaling €390 million—up 1.8% year-on-year. The Chamber’s report attributes this to ongoing investments in modernization and emissions control across several major facilities, including those operated by Northern Elements Oy and Suomi Mining Group.

The Finnish Metals Workers’ Union welcomed the figures, emphasizing the importance of predictable conditions for workforce planning. “Our members appreciate the steady pace of operations, which supports employment and community investments,” said union spokesperson Jarkko Lehtinen. “Continuous collaboration between management and workers has helped maintain safe and productive workplaces.”

Among key export destinations, Germany, Sweden, and China remained the top markets for Finnish metals and minerals. Demand for cobalt and lithium—critical for battery production—continued to rise, though at a moderate pace. “The global transition to electric mobility and renewable energy is sustaining interest in Finland’s resources, even if growth is incremental,” noted Aino Kuusela, head of external relations at the Finnish Mining Association.

Domestic consumption of steel and other construction metals also held steady, supported by ongoing infrastructure projects and housing development. The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment noted that the sector’s stable performance contributes significantly to regional economies, particularly in Lapland and Central Finland, where mining and smelting operations are primary employers.

Looking ahead, industry representatives expressed cautious optimism for the remainder of 2024. “With no major policy changes or external shocks on the horizon, we expect a similar trend of gradual growth and stable trade,” said Hietala. The Chamber of Industry and Trade is scheduled to release its next quarterly update in early October.
